edits.walkthrough_append: Worked check: name the pattern from one sketch — houses strung along a metalled road through a valley: linear; houses around a village pond or temple tank: circular; farmsteads scattered among their own fields in a forest tract: dispersed; fields touching the village on all sides with streets at right angles: rectangular. For the examination, pattern questions are answered by identification plus reason — the pattern is read from the sketch, but the cause is stated from terrain, water, defence or land division — and one reason per pattern is the difference between one mark and four.

Worked check: relabel one village by function and watch the classification follow — a Haryana village whose workers are overwhelmingly cultivators is a farming settlement; a Kerala backwater hamlet living off the lagoon is a fishing settlement; a Jharkhand settlement beside an ore pit is a mining settlement, whatever its huts look like. In the board examination, the function-versus-pattern contrast is the tested distinction: pattern is the shape on the ground, function is the work that feeds the settlement — a four-mark answer gives two definitions, one example each, and the closing line that shape follows site while function follows resources.

Worked check: place real towns on the ladder. A district headquarters with 80,000 people is Class II; a satellite town crossing 1,00,000 enters Class I and joins the million-plus club only at 10 lakh; six Indian cities have crossed the ten-million mark into megacity rank. For the examination, the class boundaries are asked cold — 1,00,000 / 50,000 / 20,000 / 10,000 / 5,000 — and higher-order questions ask what the classes are for: planning resource allocation and reading urban hierarchy, since a Class I city renders functions a Class IV town cannot. Drill the thresholds; they are pure recall marks.

Worked check: classify by the dominant employer and the name follows — Chandigarh and Bhopal exist because governments sit there (administrative); Jamshedpur and Bhilai exist because ore, coal and power met (industrial); Surat and Mumbai live by trade and finance (commercial); Varanasi and Amritsar draw their crowds on faith (religious); Shimla and Nainital on climate (tourist). For the examination, the function-classification question is answered with the category, the named Indian example, and one line on the founding cause — political decision, resource node or route intersection — because examiners award the mark for the reason as much as for the label.

Worked check: trace one problem to its cause before prescribing. Slums are not a housing failure alone but the meeting of cheap rural-urban migration with land markets that price the poor out — hence squatter settlements on the periphery and along drains. Air pollution concentrates where traffic, industry and inversion layers coincide; water shortage in cities is a supply-and-loss problem as much as a rainfall one. For the board examination, a question of the form 'discuss the problems of Indian cities' earns marks by pairing each problem with its cause and one measure — shelters, mass transit, sewers — since causes-and-remedies answers outrank lists.

Worked check: take one deficit at a time and regionalise it. Piped water and sanitation lag worst in the densely populated plain states where settlement is old and scattered; electricity supply improved fastest where feeder separation was funded; all-weather road connectivity tracks terrain and state priority. For the board examination, questions of the form 'state the problems of rural settlements' expect the standard list — poor connectivity, water and sanitation deficits, thin health and schooling services, housing quality, and livelihood strain — but full marks come from the closing sentence that rural deficits are spatially uneven, so remedies must be region-differentiated rather than uniform.

Worked check: audit one settlement against the sustainable checklist — does water supply rely on a depleting aquifer? does waste leave untreated? does commuting lock residents into fuel? does building stock survive heat without power? Each 'no' is a design task: rainwater harvesting, sewerage, transit-oriented growth, passive cooling. For the board examination, a question on sustainable cities is answered with the definition, three sectors of action — resources, mobility, housing — and one named initiative (solar rooftop mandates, metro rail, SWM rules), closing that sustainability is a design constraint on growth, not a brake upon it.

Worked check: trace one product chain to fix the sector boundaries. Cotton in the field: primary; ginned and spun into yarn: secondary; sold in a mill's showroom with credit terms: tertiary. Redi or not, the worker's task defines the sector, not the product. For the board examination, questions of the form 'what are primary activities' are answered by definition, the five sub-types — gathering and hunting, fishing, pastoralism, mining, agriculture and plantation — with one line and one region each, closing with the observation that primary activity's share falls as economies advance while its absolute output often rises.

Worked check: map the surviving hunting-gathering world — the pygmies of the Congo basin, the Bushmen of the Kalahari, the Inuit of the polar coasts, the Jarawa of the Andamans — and ask why the practice survives exactly there: harsh climate or dense forest keeps other economies out, and the environment's carrying capacity supports small, mobile groups but no more. For the board examination, the expected answer names two or three such peoples with their regions, notes the small community size and mobility, and explains persistence as adaptation rather than backwardness — a sentence examiners reward.

Worked check: read the prairies as the model case — the Canadian and American grasslands, and their southern hemisphere twins in the Argentine pampas and Australian wheat belt: vast holdings, two or three crops, machinery doing the work of a hundred hands, grain flowing by rail to ports. A single combine covering hundreds of hectares explains how one family farms what a village once did. For the board examination, the question on commercial grain farming is answered with the definition, the mid-latitude grassland locations, the four preconditions — large farms, mechanisation, temperate rainfall, market and rail access — and the yield-versus-area point that output is high by scale, not by intensity.

Worked check: follow the interdependence on one farm — maize and barley feed the cattle, cattle return manure to the fields, and the farm sells grain, milk and meat so no single price failure breaks the year; that insurance-by-diversity is the system's logic. Western Europe, and in North America the corn-and-dairy belts, supply the classic regions: deep soils, modest reliable rain, and cities close enough to take fresh milk daily. For the examination, a mixed-farming answer earns its marks by stating the interdependence, naming the regions, and giving the two locational factors — climate reliability and market proximity — with one line on risk-spreading.

Worked check: read the calendar of a Mediterranean farm — vines, olives and citrus ride out the dry summer on stored moisture or irrigation; winter grains and vegetables take the mild wet season; and the same coast sells the tourist season its produce. The combination of orchard crops, winter wheat and horticulture is the system's signature. For the board examination, a Mediterranean-agriculture answer carries the definition, the latitude band and the summer-dry rhythm, the crop list with horticulture named as the commercial core, and the closing sentence that the system marries climatic constraint to urban market demand.

Worked check: explain the siting of a Danish-style dairy belt — temperate grass, capital-heavy sheds, and the rail and refrigeration that first let butter travel to cities — and then contrast the Indian case: the same market logic runs Anand's cooperative collection vans and Bengaluru's peri-urban vegetable-and-milk farms, both serving daily demand that cannot wait. For the board examination, dairy questions are answered with the definition, the two market conditions — perishability and value-to-weight — the regions (north-west Europe, North America, Australasia), and one Indian example; the closing sentence that proximity to market, not land abundance, is the controlling factor earns the final mark.

Worked check: follow one material through the sectors — iron ore (primary) to sponge iron to rolled steel (secondary) to the dealer's warehouse (tertiary): processing adds form value at every step, which is why manufacturing is called value-addition. Note the boundary cases: a tailor and a baker are secondary — they process material into goods — while a teacher is tertiary, selling no thing at all. For the board examination, secondary-activity answers state the definition, distinguish manufacturing from crafts by scale and power, and close with the locational logic that plants sit where raw material, energy and market pull with the least total cost.

Worked check: take the classic clusters — Ludhiana's hosiery, Agra's footwear, Moradabad's brassware, Tiruppur's knitwear: thousands of small units, family labour plus a few hired hands, linked to traders who sell to national and export markets. Each cluster shows the same geography: a traditional skill, low entry capital, and a market channel that carries the town's product far beyond it. For the board examination, small-scale industry questions are answered with the definition and investment ceiling, the employment argument — jobs per rupee invested — and one named cluster as evidence that small units diffuse industry beyond the metropolitan core.

Worked check: read one plant as the type-case — a Jamshedpur-class steel works: lakhs of crores fixed in blast furnaces and rolling mills, thousands on the payroll, its own power, and a township attached. Scale is the point: fixed costs spread over millions of tonnes bring unit cost down to world-competitive levels, which is exactly why such plants must run near capacity. For the board examination, large-scale industry answers give the definition with the worker and investment thresholds, the economies-of-scale logic in one sentence, three Indian examples across iron-steel, machinery and petrochemicals, and one line on their regional pull — ports, coal belts, capitals.

Worked check: apply the least-cost idea to a real choice — a sugar mill must sit within the cane tracts because cane loses weight and sugar content every day it waits (raw-material orientated); a soft-drink bottling plant sits near consumers because its product is bulky, cheap and heavy relative to value (market orientated); a data centre follows power and connectivity instead. For the board examination, locational-factor answers are graded on this reasoning: name the factors — raw material, market, labour, power, transport, capital, agglomeration — then classify two given industries by their dominant pull, since classification is the tested skill, not the list.

Worked check: run the three factors through one decision. A garment exporter chooses Bengaluru over a cheaper town because the airport, highways and freight forwarders (transport) shave days off delivery; because buyers and design talent sit there (market and labour); and because a credit line follows the cluster's record (capital). Change any one — a new freight corridor, a dried credit line — and the map of viable locations shifts. For the board examination, answers earn marks by pairing each factor with its mechanism — access cuts cost, demand sets scale, capital sets feasibility — and illustrating all three from one named Indian industry.

Worked check: name the belts and their twin advantages — eastern North America (coal, iron, the Great Lakes and rail nexus), western and central Europe (the Ruhr's coal, the Rhine's barges), eastern Asia (Japan's Pacific belt and coastal China's deltas, ports doing the work of coalfields), and the newer belts of South and South-East Asia. For the board examination, a question of the form 'describe the major industrial regions of the world' is answered with two belts described in full — location, resources, industries — and the rest named, closing with the point that regions survive shift only by adapting when their original advantages fade.

Worked check: explain Silicon Valley's geography and the theory writes itself — university laboratories, venture capital, specialised suppliers and rivals within an hour's drive, so knowledge moves by conversation before it moves by publication; Bengaluru's software corridor repeats the pattern with engineering colleges and global clients instead. For the board examination, high-technology answers define the sector by inputs (research staff, continuous innovation) rather than outputs, contrast its location logic — skilled labour, universities, quality of life, airports — with the coal-and-iron logic of heavy industry, and close that such clusters are self-reinforcing, which is why they are hard to build and hard to kill.

Worked check: grade services by who buys and how — a barber and a street vendor sell directly to individuals (personal); a bank and an insurer sell to whoever can pay (business); a school and a public hospital are obligated to serve (public, often social overheads); and a consultancy sells expertise to firms (professional, quaternary-adjacent). For the board examination, tertiary-activity questions ask for the definition — intangible output, production and consumption together — the classification with two examples per class, and the closing generalisation that as incomes rise, the tertiary share of the workforce rises, visible in India's post-1991 services growth.

Worked check: run one trade flow through Ullman's three tests. Bangladesh needs cotton yarn it does not weave (complementarity); the yarn survives the Dhaka run because its value justifies the trucking cost (transferability); and a nearer spinning hub would take the order if one existed (intervening opportunity). Break any leg — self-sufficiency, freight above value, a closer supplier — and the flow dies. For the board examination, trade questions are answered with the definition and the basis-of-trade triad applied to a named flow, plus the India angle: composition shifting towards services and engineering goods since liberalisation.

Worked check: assign one consignment its cheapest full route — road for the first and last miles because nothing matches the door; rail for the thousand-kilometre trunk because bulk and distance beat road cost there; sea for the crossing because no alternative comes close on tonnes; air only where delay costs more than the fare — vaccines, spare parts. For the board examination, transport answers earn marks by stating the network idea — nodes, links, complementary modes — and then pricing the journey mode-by-mode, closing that each mode rules where its cost curve dips lowest.

Worked check: place one message on the spectrum — a family video call is personal communication, point to point; an all-India emergency alert is mass communication, one source to millions through radio, television and cell broadcast. Note what has changed: the smartphone has pulled mass communication into a pocket and made the receiver a sender too, while the digital divide — who has signal, data and literacy — decides who is actually reached. For the board examination, communication answers define the two forms, name the technologies in historical order from telegraph to satellite, and close on the divide, since examiners reward the equity caveat.
